The Princess ruled not through force of arms, but through an intricate web of alliances, trade agreements, and — if the more controversial historians are to be believed — genuine goodwill.

The kingdom's borders stretched from the Pipe Labyrinths in the south to the Star Road waypoints in the north. Trade caravans moved freely, protected by the Toad Guard — a civil militia more accustomed to settling disputes over market stalls than wielding weapons in anger.

Princess Peach herself was, by all surviving accounts, a ruler of remarkable complexity. The popular image — the gentle monarch in pink, eternally gracious — obscures a political mind of considerable sharpness. Palace correspondence recovered from the ruins of Toad Town reveals a leader who personally negotiated trade tariffs, who maintained a spy network that predated the Onyx Hand by decades, and who kept detailed dossiers on every noble family in the realm.

content.label: [ Examine the marginalia scrawled in the margin → ]

hidden_content.text: She also kept secrets that killed her. I found letters in the sealed vault — letters to someone she addressed only as 'T.' The handwriting trembles in places. These were not political correspondences. Chief Thornpaw of the Rakasha — his scouts confirmed at Fawful's gala what I suspected for decades. They were lovers. And someone used that love as a weapon. The secret hatch in her chambers — he knew about it because she SHOWED him. Intimacy became the murder weapon. — T.E.

content.text: The economy flourished under a coin standard backed by Star Bits — crystallized fragments of celestial energy harvested from the Star Road. A single Star Bit could power a household's heating crystal for a season, making them simultaneously currency and commodity. This dual nature would later prove catastrophic when the Star Road was severed during the wars.

The Toad populace — who comprised roughly sixty percent of the kingdom's citizens — lived in relative comfort. Mushroom houses, grown rather than built, dotted the landscape in cheerful clusters. Each settlement maintained a communal garden, a message relay station connected to the capital via warp pipe, and at least one shrine to the Star Spirits.

Yet even in this golden age, shadows gathered at the margins. The Koopa Clans to the east had unified under a warlord known only as 'the Bowser' — a title, not a name, though the distinction has been lost to common usage. The Boo Aristocracy grew increasingly isolationist, sealing their mansions behind spectral barriers. And in the deep places beneath the kingdom, in caverns lit by bioluminescent fungi, something ancient stirred.

content.title: THE STAR ROAD NETWORK
entries: Seven Star Road waypoints connected major population centers
Travel between waypoints was instantaneous but required a Star Visa
The network was maintained by the Star Spirit Council
Annual Star Bit harvest provided 73% of the kingdom's energy needs
The network's destruction in 962 BF caused the 'Long Dark' — three years without reliable power
Some believe the Star Road was destroyed deliberately to prevent escape

content.text: The final census before the assassination, conducted in 953 BF, recorded a kingdom of approximately 2.3 million souls. By the time the civil war ground to its exhausted conclusion eighty years later, that number had fallen below 800,000. Nearly two-thirds of a civilization, erased. My father called it 'the slow hemorrhage.' The kingdom did not die screaming — it bled out in the dark, one village at a time.
But I am getting ahead of myself. Before the blood, there was the betrayal. And before the betrayal, there was one final, perfect day — the last day Princess Peach would ever see.
Chapter II
content.subtitle: Highsun 1, 955 BF — The Day the Kingdom Died

content.text: he morning of Highsun 1, 955 BF began with celebrations. The Summer Solstice Festival — the kingdom's largest annual gathering — drew citizens from every province to the capital. Banners of pink and white hung from every lamppost. The smell of fire-roasted mushroom caps and Star Candy filled the streets. No one knew they were attending a funeral.

Princess Peach was scheduled to address the kingdom from the balcony of the Royal Palace at the fourteenth hour. She had done so every Highsun for the previous thirty-two years of her reign. The speech was traditionally brief — a blessing, a few words of gratitude, the ceremonial lighting of the Solstice Flame.
She never reached the balcony.

At approximately the thirteenth hour and forty minutes, while the Princess was in her private chambers completing her preparations, an unknown assailant or assailants breached the Royal Suite. The method of entry remains one of the great unsolved mysteries of our age. The suite was protected by seventeen distinct magical wards, guarded by four elite Toad Guards, and accessible only through a single reinforced door.
But there was another way in. A way known only to the Princess and those she trusted with her life. A way that does not appear on any blueprint, any ward schematic, any architectural survey.

content.label: [ A passage has been hastily glued over the original text. Carefully peel it back → ]

hidden_content.text: The secret hatch. Thornpaw told Mistveil at the gala that Peach showed it to him personally — her private escape route, her lover's entrance. Someone else learned about it. Someone close enough to discover a secret shared between a princess and her forbidden lover. The guard rotation logs show a 47-MINUTE GAP that morning — someone with authority pulled the guards away. My father's journals reference 'the arrangement.' He KNEW. The Regency KNEW. They let it happen because they stood to inherit a kingdom. — T.E., added Highsun 10, 1040 BF

content.text: The four guards were found dead at their posts, unmarked. No wounds, no poison residue, no signs of struggle. Court mages later determined they had been killed by a simultaneous cessation of all biological function — a spell so advanced that fewer than five living practitioners were believed capable of casting it. The Mages' Guild claimed jurisdiction over the magical evidence. My father let them have it. I have spent twenty years wondering why.

The Princess herself was found seated at her vanity, still holding a hairbrush. A single wound — a thin blade through the base of the skull — had killed her instantly. The precision suggested either medical knowledge or supernatural guidance. No blood had been spilled on her white dress. Whoever killed her did so with the tenderness of a lover.

The body was discovered by her handmaiden, Lady Bloomia — a young toad who had served the Princess since childhood. Bloomia's scream was heard three floors below. Within minutes, the palace was in lockdown. Within hours, the kingdom was in chaos. Within two weeks, Lady Bloomia herself had vanished.

The official record states that Lady Bloomia 'departed the capital for personal reasons.' The unofficial record — the one my father kept locked in a separate vault — tells a different story. Bloomia ran because she saw something. Or someone. And whoever she saw wanted her silenced.

content.label: [ A dried bloodstain marks this section. Beneath it, text has been scratched into the page with a pin → ]

hidden_content.text: Lady Bloomia did not simply vanish. She was HUNTED. A founding martyr of the Loyalist movement — known only as 'The Silent One' — died in the castle's servant passages protecting Bloomia's escape. She carried documents. What documents? I have searched for decades. The Loyalists believe these documents contain proof of who ordered the assassination. If Bloomia is alive, she is the most important witness in the kingdom. If she is dead, those documents are the most important evidence. Either way — FIND HER. — T.E.

content.text: What followed was not grief. Grief implies a wound that can heal. What followed was an unraveling — slow at first, then catastrophic. The Princess had no heir. No designated successor. The Council of Toads, designed to advise rather than rule, found itself thrust into a role it was neither equipped nor authorized to fill. My father, Toadsworth the Elder, stepped into the vacuum. He called it duty. Others called it opportunity.

chapters.title: Chapter III: The Century of Blood

content.text: Chapter III
content.subtitle: The Century of Blood (955–1035 BF)

content.text: ar, when it comes to the Mushroom Kingdom, does not arrive as a thunderclap. It seeps in like water through cracked stone — slowly, silently, and by the time you notice, the foundations have already given way. My father watched it happen. He could have stopped it. He chose not to, because chaos served his purpose.

The first decade of conflict (955–965 BF) is remembered as the 'War of Banners,' named for the dozens of minor lords and self-proclaimed heirs who raised their own standards and declared sovereignty over patches of territory no larger than a few villages. The Regency — MY family's Regency — could have imposed order. Instead, my father allowed the factions to exhaust themselves, ensuring that when the dust settled, only the Regency remained standing.

The official narrative blamed Bowser and the Koopa Troop for the assassination. The evidence was circumstantial — a Koopa-forged blade found near the scene, reports of Koopa scouts in the capital. Convenient. Too convenient. Bowser has denied involvement for eighty-five years, and the evidence against him has never been subjected to independent verification. Because my father's Regency controlled the investigation. Because the Mages' Guild controlled the magical evidence. Because everyone who might have contradicted the official story either vanished or died.

content.title: KEY EVENTS OF THE CENTURY WAR

events.event: Assassination of Princess Peach. Three guard witnesses give contradictory testimony.
Two guard witnesses die under suspicious circumstances. Captain Silvercap vanishes.
Lady Bloomia disappears. 'The Silent One' dies protecting her escape.
Star Road network destroyed. The Long Dark begins.
First Koopa Incursion. Eastern provinces fall within months.
Loyalist Founding Council asks 'Cui Bono?' — who benefited from Peach's death?
The Boo Aristocracy seals all mansions. Thousands of refugees turned away to die.
Battle of Pipe Junction. 40,000 casualties. The Iron Legion funded BOTH sides.
The Onyx Hand emerges. Their tribunals offer the only justice the kingdom has left.
Rise of the Iron Legion. A mercenary company becomes a state.

content.text: By the midpoint of the century, the war had evolved from territorial disputes into something more ideological. Three great power blocs had crystallized from the chaos, each believing — or claiming to believe — that they represented the kingdom's best future:

factions.name: The Peach Loyalists
factions.description: A fanatical resistance movement dedicated to avenging the Princess and uncovering the truth. Led by Captain Toadette — a woman of terrifying conviction — they have waged an unrelenting shadow war for decades. Their methods are brutal: the Bramblehaven massacre, the Toad Town coup, targeted assassinations. They call themselves freedom fighters. The Regency calls them terrorists. The truth, as always, is written in blood.

factions.name: The Iron Legion
factions.description: What began as the 'Midlands Mercenary Company' had, by 1035 BF, transformed into a military-industrial state. They controlled the Midlands with ruthless efficiency, taxed trade routes, and maintained the largest standing army in the region. Their involvement in toad trafficking — over 150 souls found hidden in barrels aboard the Vigilance — reveals the rot at their core.

factions.name: The Onyx Hand
factions.description: Neither loyalist nor legionnaire, the Onyx Hand operates in the spaces between. Part criminal syndicate, part shadow government, they control the flow of information, contraband, and — it is whispered — souls. Their vampire knights nest in places like Raventree Manor, sustained by dark crystals. Their tribunals are the only courts where a toad can receive something resembling justice.

content.label: [ A dried flower presses flat between these pages. Lift it to read what's beneath → ]

hidden_content.text: The Iron Legion funded both sides of the Battle of Pipe Junction. Forty thousand dead, and they profited from every one. But here is what haunts me: my father KNEW. I found the correspondence. The Regency received a percentage of the Legion's war profits in exchange for 'territorial non-interference.' My family is stained with the blood of forty thousand souls. And my son — Chancellor Toadsworth — inherited the arrangement. He maintains it still. The Loyalists are RIGHT to hunt us. — T.E., 1038 BF

content.text: Chapter IV
content.subtitle: The Year 1040 BF — Everything Burns

content.text: s I write these final chapters, the ink still wet on some entries, I am acutely aware that I am no longer recording history. I am watching the kingdom's death throes. Captain Toadette's Loyalists seized Toad Town on Day 12. My son is under house arrest. The Mayor is dead — executed by the Vengeance Cell. And the evidence the Loyalists found in the Regency's communication records has confirmed what I have known for twenty years: the cover-up is real, and my family built it.

The year began with a death that set everything in motion. The dragon Ignis, an ancient wyrm who had laired in the northern mountains since before the founding of the kingdom, was slain by a band of adventurers. The Mages' Guild was furious — Ignis was a living repository of arcane knowledge. But the true catastrophe came after: Fawful, the mad tactician, somehow brokered an alliance with the five remaining dragons. He walked through their fire unburned. The dragons found this... compelling.

Then came the matter of Archie Miser. Acquitted of killing a mage by an Onyx Hand tribunal, Archie became a chaos agent of staggering proportions. His actions aboard the airship Vigilance — fireballs in enclosed spaces, civilian casualties treated as acceptable collateral — embody everything that has gone wrong with our kingdom. We have become a place where violence is the default language, where diplomacy is considered weakness, where a man can kill dozens and walk free because the only court willing to hear the case is run by criminals.
The Vigilance itself became a microcosm of the kingdom's disease. In the space of thirteen days:

items.text: X.O. betrayed the crew and seized control of the ship, taking Warlord Bowser captive.
Captain Syrup was freed, turned hostile, and triggered a cascade of betrayals.
A toad named hjumpik disabled the power core with an axe — sending the ship into a nosedive.
Over 150 trafficked toads were found hidden in barrels, each sealed with Mini-Mushroom compartments.
Archie unleashed a fireball during negotiations, killing most of the Tea Leaf Syndicate's muscle.
The Iron Legion revealed their role in the trafficking and demanded prisoners be surrendered.

content.text: But it is the Loyalists' actions that will define this year in the histories yet to be written. Captain Toadette is either the kingdom's savior or its final executioner, and I am no longer certain which.

The Bramblehaven massacre haunts me. Six hundred Loyalists assaulted Fawful's fortress. Two hundred defenders — soldiers, yes, but also cooks, clerks, stable hands — were killed to the last soul. No quarter given, by Toadette's personal order. All prisoners executed. The Regal Empire has opened a formal war crimes inquiry. Toadette's response was to order further operations.

And yet — and this is the bitter irony that poisons my sleep — she may be RIGHT. The Regency covered up the assassination. My family profited from the war. The Iron Legion sold toad lives like cattle. The Mages' Guild suppressed evidence. Every institution that should have sought justice instead sought advantage, and the only people who continued demanding the truth were the ones society calls terrorists.

content.title: THE LOYALIST INVESTIGATION — KEY BREAKTHROUGHS
entries: 955 BF: Three guard witnesses give contradictory testimony. Two die within a year.
956 BF: Lady Bloomia escapes with unknown documents, protected by 'The Silent One.'
998 BF: Archivist Inkwell discovers 47-minute gap in guard rotation logs.
1010 BF: Captain Toadette recovers Toadsworth Sr.'s private journals mentioning 'the arrangement.'
1035 BF: Loyalist intelligence network confirms the Regency actively suppressed investigation leads.
1040 BF: Thornpaw reveals secret hatch and his relationship with Princess Peach.
1040 BF: Ryan's spirit vision claims to show fragmentary images of the killer's face.

content.text: The pieces are falling into place. After eighty-five years, the truth is emerging from the shadows like something that has been buried alive — decomposed but still recognizable, still reaching for the light with rotting hands.
Chapter V
content.subtitle: The Raventree Affair & The Fracturing of Reality

content.text: aventree Manor sits at a nexus of planar fractures — tears in the fabric of reality itself — that have transformed it from a mere building into a wound in the world. Ghosts walk its halls not as metaphor but as literal fact. Rooms shift and rearrange themselves. The maze in the gardens exists in multiple dimensions simultaneously. And every faction in the kingdom has converged upon it like flies on a corpse.

The reasons for this convergence are as numerous as the factions involved. The Mages' Guild sought to study — and exploit — the planar fractures. The Onyx Hand's vampire knights had established a nest within the manor, using dark crystals to sustain their undeath. The Iron Legion wanted the strategic position. Fawful's agents prowled the corridors. And the adventurers of the Vigilance — that unlikely coalition of heroes, criminals, and confused bystanders — simply tried to survive.

Luigi appeared. The brother of the legendary plumber Mario — long thought to be a figure of myth — walked through a door on the evening of Highsun 26 as if arriving for dinner. His arrival coincided with an assault by Onyx knights that forced the party to flee through windows, off verandas, and into the nightmare maze.

Remi — recruited after Wario handed her a bomb disguised as a gift — was captured by the vampire garrison. During her captivity, she discovered Green T's battle plan on a linen napkin. Archie encountered Perrius Anamatar having tea in a sitting room as reality collapsed around him. Bryan the toad arrived through a Guild portal with divination incense and a vendetta. The Purple Toad picked pockets and sang prophecies. And through it all, the parallel Dan walked the halls like a ghost who didn't know he was dead.

content.title: THE PARALLEL DAN PARADOX
entries: Dan the Toad exists in at least two simultaneous versions
The 'original' Dan is believed held by the Mages' Guild in a null cage
The 'parallel' Dan confessed his nature to Markop on Highsun 26
Dan's existence disrupts the Oracle's ability to function — the Oracle is now dead
The Mages' Guild considers Dan's elimination an acceptable cost
The implications for reality stability are described as 'catastrophic'

content.text: But it is the Mages' Guild's actions at Raventree that frighten me most. Archie overheard Luigi and a Guild member discussing plans to extract the ghosts from the manor — regardless of the cost to the living or the stability of the planar fractures. They agreed that Archie's death would be an acceptable price. They said this while he dangled from a rope above them.

The rope snapped. They noticed. And then the Guild handed Archie an itemized bill for the broken rope totaling over two thousand gold in administrative fees. This is the world we live in now: a world where bureaucrats charge murder victims for the cost of the noose.

Lady Aurelian Corvinarus made her requests — bone, ash, chalk, and iron from hjumpik. The twilight grove revealed its horrors: hunched, gray-skinned mazebounds in a forest of shadow crows and cursed artifacts. Archie was ambushed in the library by something the Guild won't name. And a spy was discovered in a ransacked sitting room, claiming to be 'looking for a toad' while the world burned around him.

content.label: [ The bottom of this page is stained with what appears to be tea. Tilt the page to read the watermarked text → ]

hidden_content.text: Fawful has allied with DRAGONS. Five of them. After we killed Ignis, he somehow brokered a deal with the remaining wyrms. He walked through their combined breath attacks unburned. No one knows how. The Star Spirits' prophecy calls him 'the one who cannot burn.' If Fawful commands dragonfire and the Guild controls planar fractures, the conventional factions — Regency, Legion, even the Loyalists — are finished. We are watching the end of the world as we know it, and most people are too busy fighting each other to look up. — T.E.

content.text: Chapter VI
content.subtitle: What My Family Has Done

content.text: have spent this entire chronicle hiding behind the historian's detachment, referring to 'the Regency' as if it were an abstraction rather than my father, my son, myself. No more. If this is to be a confession, let it be a complete one.

My father, Toadsworth the Elder, was the Royal Chamberlain on the day Princess Peach was murdered. His private journals — recovered by Captain Toadette in 1010 BF — contain references to 'the arrangement' and 'those who benefit from chaos.' I have read those journals. I know what 'the arrangement' was.

My father did not order the assassination. But he knew it was coming. He was approached — by whom, his journals do not say — and offered a choice: prevent it and remain a servant, or allow it and become a ruler. He chose power. He arranged the guard rotation gap. He ensured the investigation was compromised. He let the Mages' Guild take control of the evidence because the Guild was part of the arrangement.

He did not know about the hatch. That detail was withheld from him — insurance, perhaps, by whoever orchestrated the killing. My father provided ACCESS but not METHOD. The distinction matters legally. It does not matter morally.

content.title: FROM TOADSWORTH SR.'S PRIVATE JOURNAL
content.description: This passage was encoded using a substitution cipher where each vowel is shifted forward by one position (A→E, E→I, I→O, O→U, U→A) while consonants remain unchanged.
content.encoded_text: THI GAOLD PRIVODID THI BEDI. THI REGONCY PRIVODID THI UCCISS. O DU NUT KNUW WHU HILD THI KNOVI. BLIUMOE SEW THIM. SHI RANS.
content.solution: THE GUILD PROVIDED THE BLADE. THE REGENCY PROVIDED THE ACCESS. I DO NOT KNOW WHO HELD THE KNIFE. BLOOMIA SAW THEM. SHE RAN.
content.hint: Vowel shift: A→E, E→I, I→O, O→U, U→A. Consonants unchanged.

content.text: My son, Chancellor Toadsworth, inherited the cover-up along with the title. He maintains the Regency's arrangement with the Iron Legion. He has suppressed investigation leads. He has — I suspect — ordered the elimination of witnesses, though I cannot prove this and pray I am wrong.

When Captain Toadette seized Toad Town and placed my son under house arrest, she was not attacking an innocent government. She was dragging a guilty one into the light. The Mayor she killed had signed execution orders for three Loyalist operatives whose only crime was asking questions about the assassination. The financial ledgers the Loyalists recovered show payments from the Iron Legion to Regency officials — my son's signature on the receipts.

I am not writing this to excuse the Loyalists' methods. The Bramblehaven massacre was an atrocity. The execution of prisoners violates every law of war. Captain Toadette's fanaticism has caused as much suffering as the conspiracy she seeks to expose. But a disease is not cured by ignoring it, and the kingdom's disease has been ignored for eighty-five years.

Captain Toadette calls herself a servant of the dead Princess. She has built a movement on six sacred tenets, the first of which declares Peach eternal — not merely remembered but deified. Her operatives — Embercap, Mistveil, Bloodcap, Stonecap — kill in the Princess's name with the certainty of zealots. They leave roses at the scenes of their assassinations, thorns wet with blood.

And yet. AND YET. They are the only ones who kept looking. While my family buried the truth, while the Guild locked away the evidence, while the Legion sold toad lives for profit — the Loyalists kept searching. Archivist Inkwell found the guard rotation gap. Toadette found my father's journals. Mistveil extracted the Thornpaw revelation. They found the secret hatch. They are closer to the truth than anyone has been in eight decades.
The fanatical terrorists are the only honest people left in the kingdom. What does that say about us?
Afterword
content.subtitle: Written in Haste, Harvestide 30, 1040 BF

content.text: I set down my quill knowing this chronicle will likely be my death warrant. My son will call it treason. The Mages' Guild will call it unauthorized disclosure. The Iron Legion will call it a target acquisition. Only the Loyalists might call it what it is: the truth, delivered too late and at too great a cost.

The events at Raventree continue. Reality fractures. The Oracle is dead. A parallel Dan walks the world while the original rots in a null cage. Fawful commands dragonfire. The Mages' Guild plots extractions that could kill everyone in the manor. And somewhere — in hiding, in a grave, in a dimension that shouldn't exist — Lady Bloomia holds the final pieces of a puzzle that has consumed this kingdom for eighty-five years.

Find her. Find what she carries. Find the name of the person who walked through the secret hatch on Highsun 1, 955 BF, and put a blade through the skull of the most beloved ruler this kingdom has ever known.
Find the truth. And when you find it, do not do what my family did. Do not bury it. Do not profit from it. Do not 'arrange' it into a shape that serves your ambition.
Scream it from the highest tower. Let the kingdom hear. Let the guilty choke on it.

"The kingdom is not its borders or its crown. The kingdom is its people — stubborn, foolish, magnificent people who deserve to know what was done to them in the dark. My family stole that truth. I return it now, stained with my father's guilt and my own cowardice. May it be enough."
— END OF VOLUME ONE —

[ This volume was recovered from a hollowed-out mushroom stump near the ruins of Toad Town. The author was found dead three days later. Cause of death: spontaneous arcane feedback. The Mages' Guild described the incident as 'unrelated.' ]

books.title: Coronation Day
books.subtitle: The Lost Testimony of Lady Bloomia
books.author: Lady Bloomia (recovered manuscript)
books.description: A slim volume bound in water-stained pink silk. The handwriting grows increasingly erratic toward the end. Found in a sealed compartment in a Loyalist safehouse, this manuscript is believed to be the testimony of Lady Bloomia — Princess Peach's handmaiden who vanished after the assassination. Its authenticity is disputed. Its contents are devastating.

content.text: CORONATION DAY
The Lost Testimony of Lady Bloomia
[ AUTHENTICITY UNVERIFIED ]
Recovered from Loyalist Safehouse 'Thornwall', Harvestide 1040 BF

Archivist's note: The following manuscript was discovered sealed behind a false wall in the Loyalist safehouse designated 'Thornwall,' along with a bundle of documents bearing the Royal Seal of Princess Peach. The handwriting matches samples attributed to Lady Bloomia, Royal Handmaiden, who disappeared fourteen days after the assassination in 955 BF. Whether the author survived to the present day or composed this account shortly before her disappearance/death remains unknown.

I write this for the girl I was on the day the Princess died. She was seventeen years old. She carried a crown in a velvet case and ran up three flights of stairs because she could feel something terrible happening in her bones. She was too late. She has been too late for her entire life since.

I write this also for the dead, who cannot speak for themselves. For the four guards who died without knowing why. For the Princess who sat at her vanity and let death walk up behind her. For the Silent One who bled out in a servant's passage so that I could run away with papers that have burned a hole in my heart for decades.
"They will call this testimony unreliable. They will call me mad, or dead, or fictional. Let them. The blood on these pages is real, even if my name is not."
Chapter I
content.subtitle: Before Dawn — Highsun 1, 955 BF

content.text: woke in darkness to the sound of weeping. Soft, controlled weeping — the kind that is trying not to be heard. It came from above me, through the thin ceiling of the servants' quarters, from the direction of the Royal Suite.
The Princess was crying.

I had served her for three years. I had seen her angry, frustrated, bored, delighted, and imperiously amused. I had never heard her cry. She was not the kind of woman who cried — or so I believed. She was the kind of woman who made OTHER people cry, usually through the precise application of political pressure and a smile that could freeze lava.

I dressed quickly — white cap, pressed apron, the golden brooch that marked me as Princess's Staff — and padded barefoot through the still-dark corridors to the service lift. The palace was not yet awake. Cook Carmella's kitchen was dark. The guard posts were manned by the night shift: sleepy toads who nodded at my brooch and waved me through without interest.
When I reached the Royal Suite's service entrance, I paused. The weeping had stopped. In its place: voices. Low, urgent, intimate.

content.label: [ Press your ear to the page, as Bloomia pressed hers to the door → ]

hidden_content.text:
Two voices. Hers, and a man's. Not Toadsworth — I knew his reedy tenor. This voice was deeper, rougher, with an accent I couldn't place. They were arguing, but gently — the way people argue when they love each other too much to shout.

'You don't have to do this,' the man said.
'I do. You know I do. If they find us—'
'Let them find us. I'll fight.'
'You'll die. And then I'll die. And the kingdom dies with us.'

Silence. Then the sound of something I will not describe, because it was not meant for my ears and I have carried my shame at hearing it for decades.

content.text: I retreated to the kitchen and made her morning tea with shaking hands. Golden Sunrise blend, extra Star Bit shavings. I waited twenty minutes before returning. When I knocked, her voice answered: clear, composed, regal. As if nothing had happened. As if I had not heard her world cracking open in the dark.

She was seated at her vanity when I entered, wearing a silk robe the color of cherry blossoms. Her hair was unbound — a waterfall of gold that reached nearly to her waist. Her eyes were dry. Her smile was perfect. If I had not heard the weeping, I would never have known.
But her hands were cold when she took the teacup. Cold as river stones in winter.
"Bloomia," she said. She always used my name, never my title. It was one of the things I loved about her. "Do you know what a coronation is?"
"A ceremony of ascension, Your Highness. When a ruler accepts the crown."

"Close." She sipped her tea, staring at her reflection in the vanity mirror. "A coronation is a sacrifice. The person you were dies, and the ruler is born. You put on the crown and you surrender everything else — your name, your desires, your right to love whom you choose. You become the kingdom. And the kingdom..." She trailed off, her eyes distant. "The kingdom demands everything."
"Your Highness—"
"Do you know what today is, Bloomia?"
"The Solstice, Your Highness."
"Yes. And something else." She set down the teacup with a click that seemed too loud in the silent room. "Today is my coronation day. Again. For the last time."
I did not understand what she meant. I would not understand for decades.

content.title: BLOOMIA'S ENCODED DIARY ENTRY
content.description: Lady Bloomia kept a personal diary encoded with a simple reverse-word cipher: each word is spelled backwards.
content.encoded_text: EHS WENK EHS SAW GNIOG OT EID. EHS DLOT EM NI YREVE YAW TPECXE SDROW. I SAW OOT GNUOY OT RAEH.
content.solution: SHE KNEW SHE WAS GOING TO DIE. SHE TOLD ME IN EVERY WAY EXCEPT WORDS. I WAS TOO YOUNG TO HEAR.
content.hint: Each word is reversed. EHS = SHE, WENK = KNEW...

content.text: Chapter II
content.subtitle: The Last Dressing

content.text: helped her bathe in rosewater and Star Bit essence — a ritual cleansing traditional to the Solstice. I brushed her hair one hundred times, as her mother Queen Rose had instructed in the handmaiden's manual. I laid out her festival gown: white silk embroidered with pink mushrooms, seed pearls sewn into spiraling patterns that caught the light. The gown she would die in.

She was quiet throughout. Normally, Princess Peach chattered during her preparations — palace gossip, policy concerns, barbed observations about visiting dignitaries that would make me choke back laughter. That morning, she stared at her reflection as if trying to memorize her own face.
"Bloomia." She said my name differently now. Softer. "If something were to happen to me — no, don't look at me like that, it's hypothetical — if something happened, what would you do?"
"I would mourn you, Your Highness. And then I would find whoever was responsible."

She smiled — a real smile, the kind that reached her eyes and made them bright with something I now recognize as sorrow. "Loyal to the end. You remind me of someone." She touched her throat, where I noticed for the first time a faint mark — the impression of a chain recently removed. She had been wearing something around her neck. Something she had taken off before I arrived.

content.title: THE PRINCESS'S MORNING — RECOVERED SCHEDULE
entries: Before 5th hour: Unknown visitor in chambers (Bloomia's testimony)
5th hour: Morning tea and preparation begins
7th hour: Festival gown fitting. Princess asks about death (hypothetical).
9th hour: Crown delivery requested from Royal Vault
10th hour: Bloomia sent to retrieve crown — NOTE: this removed her from the suite
11th hour: Unknown events in Royal Suite (47-minute guard gap begins)
13th hour, 40 minutes: Assassination occurs
14th hour: Bloomia discovers body

content.text: She sent me away three times that morning. Each time for a plausible reason — fetch a different pair of shoes, check on the crown, confirm a detail with the kitchen. Each time I returned, something in the room had changed. A drawer left ajar. A faint smell of earth and pine that did not belong in a perfumed royal suite. The impression of a large body in the cushions of the settee.
Someone was visiting her. Someone who came and went through a passage I could not see. Someone she was protecting — from me, from the guards, from the world.
The third time she sent me away, she took my hands. Hers were still cold — colder, even, as if the warmth were draining out of her slowly, as if she were already beginning to die.
"Go to the vault," she said. "Fetch the Solstice Crown yourself. Don't trust the pages. Don't trust the guards. Go yourself, see it with your own eyes, and bring it directly to me."
"Your Highness, is something—"

"Bloomia." Her grip tightened. Her eyes bore into mine with an intensity that made my breath catch. "When you return, if anything seems... wrong... do not enter the suite. Go directly to the servant passages. There is a loose stone in the third corridor, left side, behind the tapestry of the Star Festival. Behind it, you will find a leather case. Take it and RUN. Do you understand?"
"Your Highness, you're frightening me."
"Good. Fear will keep you alive. Promise me, Bloomia."
"I promise."
She released my hands. The mask of composure slid back into place. "Excellent. Now go. And take your time — I need an hour alone."

content.label: [ A section of the page has been torn and reattached. Read the hidden fragment → ]

hidden_content.text:
She was giving me an escape route. The leather case behind the loose stone — she had PREPARED it. She knew what was coming. She knew the day, the hour, the method. She was not a victim caught unaware. She was a woman walking deliberately into death and making sure her secrets survived even if she did not. She chose the Solstice because eighty thousand people would be watching the balcony, not the chambers. She chose ME because I was young enough to be overlooked and loyal enough to run.

But she didn't tell me WHY. And that silence has been the cruelest wound of all.

content.text: Chapter III
content.subtitle: The Vault and the Guild

content.text: he Royal Vault lay three floors beneath the palace, accessible only through a winding stair guarded at five separate checkpoints. I passed through each one with my golden brooch held high, my heart hammering, the Princess's words echoing in my skull: 'Do not trust the guards.'

The vault master was an ancient toad named Cornelius, whose spots had faded to near-invisibility and whose hands shook with palsy but whose mind remained diamond-sharp. When I arrived, I found him arguing with two figures in dark robes embroidered with silver staves.
Mages' Guild.
"The seals are perfectly intact!" Cornelius was saying. "I've inspected them three times. There is NO irregularity."

"Our instruments disagree," the taller mage replied. He was silver-haired, pale-eyed, with the particular condescension that the Guild cultivates like a hothouse flower. "Traces of unauthorized magical access. The crown cannot be released until we complete our investigation."
I stepped forward. "The Princess requires the crown immediately."
The tall mage turned. He looked through me the way mages look through anyone who cannot cast. "The handmaiden. Bloomia, yes?"
How did he know my name?

content.title: GUILD MAGE'S CONCEALED NOTATION
content.description: Bloomia later found this notation scratched into the vault's visitor log in a cipher the Guild uses for field communications. Each letter is replaced by its position number in the alphabet.
content.solution: SUBJECT IS AWARE. THE HATCH IS OPEN. PROCEED AS PLANNED.

content.text: "Tell me, Bloomia," the tall mage continued, "in your time serving the Princess, have you noticed anything unusual? Visitors at odd hours? Passages that seem to lead nowhere? Smells that don't belong?"
My blood ran cold. He was describing exactly what I had noticed that morning. The earth-and-pine smell. The shifted cushions. The passages she kept sending me away from. He KNEW.
"No," I said. "Nothing unusual."
He smiled. The smile of a predator who has confirmed the location of its prey. "Of course not. Well, take the crown. We were just leaving."

They stepped aside. Cornelius, his hands trembling harder than usual, retrieved the Solstice Crown from its enchanted case. As he placed it in the velvet carrying case, he leaned close and whispered: "Run, child. Don't look back. Something is very wrong today."
I took the crown. I ran.

Five checkpoints. Three flights of stairs. The tall mage's voice floated after me, casual and terrible: "Be careful, Bloomia. The wards have been behaving strangely today. Fluctuations in the protective enchantments."
He was warning me. Not out of kindness — out of cruelty. He wanted me to know that something was happening and that I could not stop it.

content.label: [ The ink here changes color — written at a different time. Read the addition → ]

hidden_content.text:
I know his name now. The tall mage. His name was Valorian Stormweave, Senior Enforcer of the Mages' Guild. He was in the vault that morning because the Guild was PART OF IT. They disabled the wards. They detected the hatch opening and did nothing. They delayed the crown to keep me away from the suite during the killing.

Valor Stormweave lived for eighty-five more years after helping murder my Princess. He was eventually killed by a mage named Archie Miser in a public market — 'justifiable magical defense,' the Onyx Hand ruled. I do not know Archie Miser. But I owe him a debt he will never know about.

The only man who could have testified about what the Guild knew that morning is now ash. Convenient. Very convenient. — B.

content.text: Chapter IV
content.subtitle: What I Found

content.text: he silence was the first thing I noticed. Not the comfortable silence of rest but the silence of aftermath — the silence that settles over a battlefield after the last scream fades. The corridor outside the Royal Suite was empty. No guards. Not sleeping, not distracted — simply gone. Four posts, four empty chairs, four abandoned weapons propped against the wall.
No. Not abandoned. Placed. Carefully, precisely, as if arranged for a painting. The weapons were parallel. The chairs were evenly spaced. Someone had STAGED this absence.
The Princess's words slammed into me: 'If anything seems wrong, do not enter the suite.'

I should have obeyed. I should have gone to the servant passages, found the loose stone, taken the leather case, and run. That was what she wanted. That was the plan she had made for me — the plan she had made because she knew she was going to die.
I pushed open the door instead. Because I was seventeen. Because I loved her. Because I thought that if I was fast enough, brave enough, loyal enough, I could still save her.

The guards were in the outer chamber. Four toads, crumpled at their posts. Their eyes were open. Their expressions were peaceful — not the frozen terror of violent death, but the blankness of someone who had simply... stopped. No wounds. No blood. No signs of struggle. They had been turned off like candles.

I crossed the outer chamber. The receiving room. The door to her private quarters, standing ajar by exactly three inches — enough to see through, not enough to enter comfortably. As if left open deliberately. As if inviting me to look.
I looked.

She was seated at her vanity. The hairbrush was still in her hand. Her eyes were closed. The white silk gown I had buttoned that morning was pristine — not a wrinkle, not a stain, not a single drop of blood on the white fabric. She looked like she was sleeping.

But her head was tilted at an angle that no sleeping person would choose. And there was a thin line of red at the base of her skull, barely visible beneath the curtain of her golden hair. A precise wound. A professional wound. The work of someone who knew exactly where to place a blade to end a life instantly, painlessly, without disturbing the body's repose.
Someone who cared enough to make it gentle.

I screamed. The sound tore from my throat like something alive — a raw, animal shriek that echoed through the empty suite and out into the corridors. I dropped the crown case. I fell to my knees. I screamed until my voice shattered and all that came out was a thin, reedy whistle of agony.
And then I saw the hatch.

content.label: [ Bloomia has crossed out the next paragraph multiple times. Reconstruct the text → ]

hidden_content.text:
Behind her vanity, the portrait of Queen Portabella was askew. Behind the portrait: a dark opening in the wall, barely large enough for a person to crawl through. Air moved through it — cold air, smelling of earth and pine and something else. Something copper. Something animal.

Blood. Not hers — hers had barely been spilled. Someone ELSE'S blood, on the edges of the hatch. The assassin had cut themselves entering or leaving. There was a partial handprint — too large for a toad, too small for a koopa.

A HUMAN handprint. Pressed in blood against the stone.

I have never told anyone this. The official investigation found the hatch but somehow missed the handprint. Or they cleaned it. Or they lied.

content.text: Chapter V
content.subtitle: The Leather Case and the Silent One

content.text: uards came running. Mages arrived. The palace erupted into controlled chaos — emphasis on 'controlled.' Because even in those first frantic minutes, I noticed something: the people taking charge were not the people who SHOULD have been taking charge. The Captain of the Guard was absent. The Chamberlain — Toadsworth the Elder — arrived twenty minutes late, looking not shocked but RESIGNED.

They wrapped me in a blanket. Someone pushed cold tea into my hands. They asked me questions — what did I see, what did I hear, when did I arrive. I answered mechanically, my eyes fixed on the door to her chambers, where mages in Guild robes were casting spells that filled the air with colored light.

But I was watching the Chamberlain. Toadsworth the Elder stood in the corner, speaking in low tones with the tall mage from the vault. The one who knew my name. The one who had smiled like a predator. They were not exchanging shock and grief. They were exchanging INSTRUCTIONS.
The Princess's words hit me like a hammer blow: 'Loose stone. Third corridor. Leather case. RUN.'

I stood up. I mumbled something about needing air. No one tried to stop me — I was a seventeen-year-old handmaiden in shock, not a threat, not important, not worth watching. That was the mistake that saved my life.

content.title: CONTENTS OF THE LEATHER CASE (PARTIAL INVENTORY)
entries: Sealed letters bearing Princess Peach's personal cipher (not the Royal Seal)
A list of names, some crossed out, with dates beside each
A pressed flower — species unknown, possibly from the Rakasha territories
A sketch of the secret hatch's mechanism, annotated in two handwritings
A small vial containing a dark liquid (alchemical analysis inconclusive)
A single page torn from a larger document, bearing the words: 'THEY WILL BLAME THE KOOPAS'
A gold chain with a pendant — the chain the Princess removed before Bloomia arrived

content.text: I found the loose stone. I found the leather case. It was heavier than I expected — packed tight with documents, sealed letters, a vial of something dark, and a gold chain with a pendant that I recognized: the Princess had worn it every day for as long as I had served her. She had removed it that morning. She had hidden it here, along with everything else, because she knew she would not need it again.

I was in the servant passages, clutching the case to my chest, when I heard footsteps. Not the soft padding of servants — the deliberate, measured tread of someone who knows exactly where they are going. Someone who knew about the passages. Someone who was looking for me.

I ran. The passages twisted through the castle's walls like veins through a body — narrow, dark, branching unpredictably. I knew them well enough to navigate by touch, but whoever followed me knew them too. Every turn I took, the footsteps adjusted. Every corridor I chose, they anticipated.
I would have been caught. I would have died in those dark passages with the Princess's secrets clutched to my chest, another inconvenient witness silenced, another loose end tidied away.

But someone else was in the passages that day. Someone I never saw clearly — a shape in the darkness, broad-shouldered, moving with the quiet efficiency of a soldier. They stepped between me and my pursuer, and I heard sounds that I will not describe in detail. Sounds of violence. Sounds of sacrifice.

The Silent One. The founding martyr of the Loyalist movement. They died in that corridor so that I could live. I never learned their name. I never saw their face. I heard them die — a choking gasp, a thud, the wet sound of a blade being withdrawn — and then silence. The pursuing footsteps did not continue. My protector had bought my escape with their life.

content.label: [ Tear stains have blurred this section. Wait for them to dry → ]

hidden_content.text:
I think about the Silent One every day. Who were they? How did they know I would be in the passages? Had the Princess TOLD someone to protect me? Was this part of her plan — save the handmaiden, save the evidence, let the rest burn?

The Loyalists honor them as a founding martyr. They do not know what I know: that the Silent One killed at least two pursuers before dying. I heard the bodies fall. When I looked back — just once, just briefly — I saw dark shapes on the ground. One of them wore Guild robes.

A MAGES' GUILD OPERATIVE was hunting me in the servant passages within an hour of the assassination. The Guild was not investigating the crime. They were CLEANING UP AFTER IT.

chapters.title: Chapter VI: What the Documents Reveal

content.text: Chapter VI
content.subtitle: The Princess's Evidence

content.text: have spent years studying the documents the Princess left for me. Some are in her personal cipher — a code I have only partially broken. Some are in plain language that is worse than any cipher because the words say things I do not want to understand. Here is what I know:

Princess Peach discovered a conspiracy against her life approximately six months before the assassination. She did not know the exact date it would occur, but she knew the method (the hatch), the facilitators (the Mages' Guild and members of her own court), and the likely aftermath (civil war). She could not prevent it because the conspirators included people she could not remove without triggering the very crisis she sought to avoid.

The page torn from a larger document — the one that reads 'THEY WILL BLAME THE KOOPAS' — is written in a hand that is not hers. Someone warned her. Someone inside the conspiracy told her what was coming, and she could do nothing but prepare her escape route for others and walk into death with her eyes open.

The list of names is the most disturbing document. Fifteen names, arranged in three columns. The first column is headed 'KNEW.' The second: 'HELPED.' The third: 'HELD THE BLADE.' Several names are crossed out — people who died before the assassination of natural or 'natural' causes. Others remain. Some I recognize. Some I do not.

content.title: THE PRINCESS'S PERSONAL CIPHER
content.description: The following passage from the Princess's sealed letters uses a cipher based on the word MUSHROOM — each letter shifts by the corresponding position of letters in the keyword (M=13, U=21, S=19, H=8, R=18, O=15, O=15, M=13, cycling).
content.encoded_text: VBL EVWXJ TXAM SV PGDM. RW TH S ASIVXUZM.
content.solution: I CHOSE THIS DEATH. IT IS A SACRIFICE.

content.text: The vial. The small dark vial in the leather case. I had it analyzed by an alchemist I trust — one of the few people who knows I am alive. The liquid inside is a concentrated extract of Nightshade and Star Bit, combined in proportions that should be impossible. The alchemist called it 'liquid choice.'
If consumed, it would kill painlessly within seconds. The Princess had an alternative to the blade. She chose not to use it.

Why? Because the assassination had to look like murder, not suicide. Because a kingdom mourns a murdered princess and demands justice. A kingdom that loses its ruler to despair simply... moves on. She needed the kingdom to be ANGRY. She needed the conspirators to be HUNTED. She needed the truth to claw its way out of the grave they dug for it, even if it took a century.

She chose to be killed by someone she trusted. She sat at her vanity and let them walk up behind her through the hatch she had shown to her lover — the hatch that was supposed to be her escape, repurposed as her executioner's entrance. She held her hairbrush and waited for the blade.

And she left me the evidence. Because she knew that someone, someday, would be fanatical enough to keep looking. Someone like Captain Toadette, who built a movement on the Princess's memory and turned her death into a religion.

content.label: [ The last item in the leather case. Examine it → ]

hidden_content.text: The gold chain. The pendant the Princess wore every day and removed that morning. I have worn it against my skin for decades. It is warm to the touch — always warm, even in winter. Inside the pendant is a miniature portrait, painted with such precision that it must have been done by magical means.

The portrait shows two figures: Princess Peach and Chief Thornpaw of the Rakasha. They are holding hands. They are smiling. They look like two people who thought love would be enough to save them.

It wasn't. Love does not stop blades. Love does not undo conspiracies. Love does not prevent kingdoms from burning. But she wore his image over her heart until the very last day, and she hid it where her killers would never find it.

The third column on her list — 'HELD THE BLADE' — contains only one name. I will not write it here. Not yet. Not until I am certain it can be used. But I will say this: it is not the name anyone expects. It is not a koopa. It is not a mage. It is someone the Princess loved. Someone she forgave, even as they killed her.

Some sacrifices require a willing executioner.

content.text: Chapter VII
content.subtitle: Why I Disappeared

content.text: ourteen days. That is how long I survived in the open after the assassination. Fourteen days of questioning, of sympathetic guards bringing me tea, of Guild mages asking gently probing questions about what I had seen. Fourteen days during which I realized, with growing horror, that everyone around me was performing a script.

The investigation was a pantomime. Leads were followed and then abandoned. Evidence was collected and then lost. The three guards who had been on perimeter duty that night — the only witnesses besides me — gave testimony that contradicted each other in specific, calculated ways. As if they had been told to be unreliable.

On Day 7, the Mages' Guild assumed control of the investigation, citing 'jurisdictional concerns regarding magical evidence.' That same day, two of the three guard witnesses died. One fell from a tower. One choked on a bone at dinner. The third — Captain Silvercap — vanished overnight, leaving no trace.
They were cleaning house. The witnesses were being eliminated, one by one, in ways designed to look accidental. And I was next.

Toadsworth the Elder named Acting Regent. Investigation 'scaled back.'
Bloomia notices she is being followed.
Bloomia disappears. Official explanation: 'personal reasons.'

content.text: I noticed them on Day 12. Shadows that moved when I moved. Faces that appeared in crowds and then vanished. The faint hum of a tracking enchantment that I could feel in my teeth — a Mages' Guild specialty, I would later learn.

On the night of Day 14, I packed the leather case, wrapped the Princess's pendant around my neck, and climbed out of my window into a gutter that led to the castle's drainage system. I crawled through filth and darkness for three hours until I emerged in the forest outside the capital walls. I walked for six days without stopping, eating what I could find, sleeping in ditches, trusting no one.

I have been walking ever since. For decades now. Different names, different faces, different cities. The leather case travels with me always, wrapped in enchantment-blocking cloth I purchased from a hedge witch in the Bob-omb region. The documents inside are the only proof that the assassination of Princess Peach was not an act of foreign aggression but an inside job — a conspiracy of her own court, her own protectors, her own Guild.

content.text: To the Loyalists who will find this manuscript: I know what you are. I know what Captain Toadette has done in the Princess's name — the massacres, the executions, the fanaticism that has turned a quest for justice into a religion of blood. The Princess would not have wanted this. But the Princess is dead, and the dead do not get to choose how they are mourned.
Final Words
content.subtitle: For Those Who Continue the Search

content.text: I am old now, if I am alive at all. The Princess's pendant still hangs warm against my chest. The leather case still sits within arm's reach. The documents inside have yellowed but remain legible. The name in the third column — 'HELD THE BLADE' — burns in my memory like a brand.

I will not write that name in this manuscript. Not because I am afraid, but because naming the killer without the supporting evidence would allow the conspirators to discredit the accusation and destroy what remains. The name must be revealed alongside the documents, in a setting where it cannot be suppressed or denied.

What I will tell you is this: the killer loved the Princess. The killing was an act of mercy — or so the killer believed. The Princess knew who would hold the blade. She chose them. She sat at her vanity and waited because she trusted no one else to make her death swift and painless.
She was murdered by someone she loved, at her own request, for reasons I have spent a lifetime trying to understand.

The title of this manuscript — 'Coronation Day' — is what the Princess called that morning. 'Today is my coronation day,' she told me. 'Again. For the last time.' I understand now what she meant. The Solstice ceremony was a renewal of the monarch's bond with the kingdom. Each year, the Princess symbolically died as a person and was reborn as the Crown. That final morning, she chose to make the metaphor literal.
She crowned herself in death. She became eternal — not a ruler but a symbol, not a woman but a cause. She gave the kingdom something more powerful than a living monarch: a martyr.
"The crown that is shattered cannot be saved. But the fragments cut deeper than the whole ever could."
— THE CROWN ENDURES —
[ Find the place where roses grow in winter. Bring proof of loyalty. I will be waiting. ]
[ — Lady Bloomia, date unknown — ]

content.text: PROTOCOLS OF SHADOW
Internal Codex of the Onyx Hand
Compiled by Judge Obsidian
For Initiates of the Third Circle and Above

You hold in your hands a document that does not exist. The Onyx Hand keeps no records. We leave no traces. We cast no shadows — for we ARE the shadow. If you are reading this, you have either earned our trust through years of service, or you have made a very grave mistake.

The protocols contained herein govern our operations, our tribunals, and our sacred duty to maintain balance in a kingdom that has forgotten what balance means. We are not criminals, though the surface world names us such. We are the necessary darkness that defines the light.
"In the absence of justice, we provide order. In the absence of order, we provide consequences."
content.attribution: — The First Judge, founding declaration, 1015 BF

chapters.title: Chapter I: Structure of the Hand

content.text: Chapter I
content.subtitle: Structure of the Hand

content.text: he Onyx Hand operates through a system of concentric circles, each with its own responsibilities, privileges, and — most importantly — limitations on knowledge. What you know depends on where you stand. This is not cruelty; it is protection. The less you know, the less you can betray.

The outermost circle — the First — comprises our eyes and ears. Informants, merchants, beggars, servants. They do not know they serve us. They simply... talk. And we listen. Every tavern conversation, every pillow whisper, every drunken confession flows upward through channels they cannot see.

The Second Circle consists of our hands — the operatives who act upon gathered intelligence. Thieves, smugglers, enforcers. They know they serve the Hand, but they do not know who gives the orders. They receive instructions through dead drops, coded messages, anonymous couriers. They are skilled, loyal, and utterly expendable.

content.title: THE FIVE CIRCLES
entries: First Circle: Unknowing informants and assets
Second Circle: Field operatives and enforcers
Third Circle: Cell leaders and regional coordinators
Fourth Circle: The Tribunal — judges who dispense shadow justice
Fifth Circle: [REDACTED] — existence unconfirmed

content.text: You, initiate, have been elevated to the Third Circle. You will coordinate operations within your assigned territory. You will never meet your counterparts. You will never know how many of us exist. You will report to a voice through a speaking stone, and you will obey without question.

The Fourth Circle comprises the Tribunal — the judges who hear cases that the surface world cannot or will not adjudicate. When the Mages' Guild demands internal arbitration for a murderer, when the Iron Legion's soldiers commit atrocities without consequence, when the powerful crush the weak with impunity... the Tribunal provides an alternative.

Our justice is not gentle. It is not forgiving. But it is FAIR. The Tribunal weighs evidence without regard for wealth, faction, or species. A koopa stands equal to a toad in our courts. A mage's arcane credentials carry no weight against a farmer's honest testimony.

content.label: [ A page has been folded and sealed with black wax. Break the seal → ]

hidden_content.text: The Fifth Circle exists. I have seen the chamber beneath the chamber. Five thrones, five figures, faces hidden even from the Tribunal. They do not judge — they DECIDE. Wars have ended because they willed it. Factions have risen and fallen at their word. I do not know their names. I do not know if they are mortal. I know only that they have watched this kingdom since before the Princess died, and they will watch it long after we are dust. — J.O.

content.text: As a Third Circle operative, you may petition the Tribunal on behalf of those who cannot reach us through normal channels. This is a sacred responsibility. Abuse it, and you will discover that our justice applies to our own as readily as to outsiders.

chapters.title: Chapter II: The Archie Miser Precedent

content.text: Chapter II
content.subtitle: The Archie Miser Precedent

content.text: n Highsun 2, 1040 BF, the Tribunal rendered a verdict that would reshape our relationship with every major faction in the kingdom. The case of Archie Miser — a mage who killed a fellow practitioner — tested the boundaries of our authority and exposed the rot at the heart of the Mages' Guild.

The facts were these: Archie Miser, a human mage of considerable but undisciplined power, engaged in lethal combat with a Guild-credentialed practitioner named Valorian Stormweave. The confrontation occurred in a public market. Seven bystanders were injured. Stormweave died from a combination of fire damage and blunt force trauma when Archie threw him through a load-bearing wall.

The Mages' Guild demanded Archie be surrendered to their internal courts — courts notorious for protecting their own at the expense of outsiders. They cited ancient charter rights. They threatened economic sanctions. They hinted at arcane retaliation.
We told them no.

The trial lasted six hours. Twenty-three witnesses testified. Evidence included scrying reconstructions, physical artifacts, and testimony from two of the injured bystanders. The Tribunal — three judges whose identities remain protected — deliberated for forty-seven minutes before rendering their verdict.
"The killing of Valorian Stormweave constitutes justifiable magical defense. The deceased initiated hostilities with lethal intent. The defendant responded with proportionate force. ACQUITTED."

The Guild's response was immediate and furious. Three observers walked out during the verdict reading. One — a senior enforcer named Magistrix Vellum — was later found dead in her quarters, cause of death listed as 'spontaneous arcane feedback.' The Guild blamed us. We had nothing to do with it.

content.label: [ A notation in different handwriting appears in the margin. Examine it → ]

hidden_content.text: We had EVERYTHING to do with it. Vellum was preparing to expose the Tribunal's location to Guild strike teams. The Fifth Circle authorized her elimination. I was the one who modified her focusing crystal to overload. May her soul find whatever peace awaits oath-breakers. — Agent Whisper

content.text: The Archie Miser case established several crucial precedents:

items.text: The Onyx Hand Tribunal has jurisdiction over any crime committed within unaligned territory, regardless of the perpetrator's factional affiliation.
Guild charter rights do not supersede universal principles of self-defense.
Economic and arcane threats will not influence Tribunal verdicts.
Those who attempt to subvert our justice will face consequences.

content.text: Archie Miser walked free. He has since become a chaos agent of significant concern — his actions aboard the Vigilance and at Raventree Manor have killed dozens. Some within our ranks question whether the acquittal was wise. But wisdom was never the point. JUSTICE was the point. And justice, unlike wisdom, does not concern itself with consequences.
Chapter III
content.subtitle: The Vampire Question

content.text: ithin our ranks, a transformation is occurring that demands acknowledgment. The Onyx Knights — our elite enforcement arm — have increasingly turned to vampirism as a means of enhancing their capabilities. This document will address the theological, practical, and strategic implications of this development.

Let us be clear: the Onyx Hand does not officially sanction vampirism. We do not recruit vampires. We do not create vampires. What we DO acknowledge is that certain operatives, in pursuit of their duties, have accepted the dark gift from sources outside our organization. These operatives retain their positions so long as they adhere to strict protocols.

content.title: VAMPIRE OPERATIVE PROTOCOLS
entries: Feeding is permitted only from willing donors or condemned criminals
Creation of new vampires requires Fifth Circle authorization
Sustaining crystals must be registered with regional coordinators
Daylight operations require specialized equipment and advance notice
Failure to control blood hunger results in immediate termination

content.text: The advantages are undeniable. Vampire operatives possess enhanced strength, speed, and sensory capabilities. They do not age. They can survive injuries that would kill mortal agents ten times over. In a war of shadows, such advantages matter.

The risks, however, are equally significant. Vampires require sustenance that creates dependencies and vulnerabilities. Their aversion to sunlight limits operational flexibility. And the psychological changes that accompany the transformation — the hunger, the detachment from mortal concerns, the gradual erosion of empathy — can compromise an operative's judgment.

Recent events at Raventree Manor have thrown these concerns into sharp relief. Our vampire knights established a nest within the manor, using dark crystals to sustain their undeath and coordinate operations against multiple factions. The strategy was sound. The execution was flawless. And then everything went wrong.

A battle plan discovered by the prisoner Remi detailed an assault strategy to destroy the sustaining crystals and eliminate our knights. The plan originated with Green T of the Tea Leaf Syndicate — an organization we had considered neutralized. Their survival, and their knowledge of our crystal network, suggests a security breach of concerning proportions.

content.label: [ Blood stains obscure part of this page. Carefully clean them to read → ]

hidden_content.text: Knight-Captain Sanguine's final report, recovered from Raventree: 'They know about the crystals. They know about the Fifth Circle. Someone inside the Hand is feeding them information. I am compiling a list of suspects but I fear I will not survive to—' The report ends here. Sanguine's ashes were found scattered across three rooms. We have a traitor. — J.O.

content.text: Until the traitor is identified and eliminated, all vampire operations are suspended. Sustaining crystals are to be relocated to secondary sites. Knight-operatives are to operate independently, without coordination through normal channels. Trust no one. Suspect everyone.
Chapter IV
content.subtitle: The Coming Storm

content.text: ntelligence gathered over the past season paints a picture of converging catastrophes. The planar fractures at Raventree Manor are not an isolated phenomenon — they are symptoms of a deeper instability that threatens the fabric of reality itself. The Oracle is dead. The parallel entities multiply. And Fawful has allied with dragons.
The Fifth Circle has issued a rare directive: all resources are to be redirected toward intelligence gathering on three priority targets.

factions.name: Fawful's Dragon Alliance
factions.description: The mad tactician has somehow brokered an alliance with the remaining dragon flights. After the death of Ignis, the dragons were expected to retreat further into isolation. Instead, they have found a champion willing to wage war on their behalf. Fawful commands strategic brilliance and bottomless spite. The dragons command fire that can melt fortress walls. Together, they pose an existential threat.

factions.name: The Mages' Guild Extraction Team
factions.description: Guild operatives are preparing to extract the ghosts from Raventree Manor — regardless of the cost to the living or the stability of the planar fractures. Their motives remain unclear. The ghosts may contain knowledge, power, or something else entirely. What is clear is that the extraction will cause massive collateral damage, and the Guild considers this acceptable.

factions.name: The Parallel Dan Anomaly
factions.description: Dan the Toad exists in two places simultaneously. The original is held in a Mages' Guild null cage. The parallel walks free, disrupting the Oracle's function and destabilizing local reality. The Guild wants him dead. The Loyalists want him protected. We want to understand what he IS — because whatever created him may be capable of creating more.

content.text: The Fifth Circle's analysis suggests these three threats are connected. Fawful's timing — allying with dragons immediately after Ignis's death — implies foreknowledge. The Guild's urgency regarding Raventree extraction suggests they know something about the planar fractures that they are not sharing. And Dan's existence may be neither accident nor experiment, but the first sign of a larger phenomenon.

Our working theory: someone or something is deliberately destabilizing reality in preparation for a larger event. The assassination of Princess Peach eighty-five years ago may have been the first move in a game we are only now beginning to perceive.

events.event: Princess Peach assassinated through impossible means
Star Road network destroyed — coincidence or preparation?
Onyx Hand founded — were we created to serve this pattern?
Iron Legion consolidates — another prepared piece?
Convergence at Raventree — the endgame begins?

content.text: If this pattern holds, we are not players in this game. We are pieces. And pieces do not get to choose their moves.
Unless they learn the rules.
Appendix
